title: Replacement of complexes by degree-zero objects for a bounded degree function
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category [def-sp-abelian], and use integer-indexed cochain complexes and quasi-isomorphisms [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $d:\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal A)\to\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$ and let $D\geq0$ be an integer such that $d(A)\leq D$ for every object $A$. Suppose that every object embeds in an object $I$ with $d(I)=0$, that $d(A\oplus B)\leq\max\{d(A),d(B)\}$, and that every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ satisfies $d(C)\leq\max\{d(A)-1,d(B)\}$, where subtraction in $\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$ is truncated at zero. Then for every cochain complex $K^\bullet$ there are a cochain complex $L^\bullet$ and a quasi-isomorphism $K^\bullet\to L^\bullet$ such that $d(L^r)=0$ for every $r\in\mathbf Z$.

source.place: Tag 07K6, lemma-replace-resolution; bounded-degree specialization, since r+d(K^r)≤r+D tends to minus infinity as r tends to minus infinity.

proof.text: First $d(0)=0$: choose a degree-zero object $I$ using the embedding hypothesis for the zero object and apply the short-exact-sequence inequality to $0\to I\xrightarrow{1}I\to0\to0$. If $A\cong B$, apply that inequality to $0\to0\to A\to B\to0$ and to the inverse isomorphism to obtain $d(B)\leq d(A)$ and $d(A)\leq d(B)$. Thus $d$ is invariant under isomorphism, in particular on all zero objects. If $D=0$, every term already has degree zero, and the identity of $K$ is the required quasi-isomorphism. Henceforth suppose $D>0$ and set $\mathcal I=\{A:d(A)=0\}$. It contains the zero object and every object embeds into a member.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), hypotheses and the class of degree-zero objects; preliminary consequences of the short-exact inequality.

proof.text: Let $T$ be the brutal lower truncation of $K$ at zero: $T^r=0$ for $r<0$, $T^r=K^r$ for $r\geq0$, with the inherited differentials in nonnegative degrees. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-subcategory-right-resolution-05T6] with $a=0$ and the class $\mathcal I$ from Step 1. It supplies a termwise monomorphic quasi-isomorphism $\sigma:T\to M$ with $M^r=0$ for $r<0$ and $d(M^r)=0$ for every $r$. Form $J$ by retaining $K^r$ for $r<0$, taking $M^r$ for $r\geq0$, and using $\sigma^0d_K^{-1}$ for the differential from degree $-1$ to degree $0$. The identity below zero and $\sigma$ above it give $\alpha:K\to J$. This is a chain map, since $d_M^0\sigma^0d_K^{-1}=\sigma^1d_K^0d_K^{-1}=0$. For $r\leq-2$ the cohomology is unchanged; for $r=-1$ it is unchanged because $\sigma^0$ is mono. At $r=0$, the map $\ker d_K^0\to\ker d_M^0$ induced by $\sigma^0$ is an isomorphism, since it is $H^0(\sigma)$ for the lower-truncated complexes; it identifies the images of the incoming degree $-1$ differentials and therefore induces an isomorphism on their quotients. For $r\geq1$, $H^r(\alpha)=H^r(\sigma)$. Hence $\alpha$ is a quasi-isomorphism. We have $d(J^r)=0$ for $r\geq0$, and still $d(J^r)\leq D$ for all $r$.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), first proof paragraph; Tag 05T6 (lemma-subcategory-right-resolution), part (1).

proof.text: We now give the elementary replacement used on any current complex $C$. Choose an index $n$ with $d(C^n)>0$, and a monomorphism $j:C^n\to E$ with $d(E)=0$. Put $P=\operatorname{Coker}((j,-d_C^n):C^n\to E\oplus C^{n+1})$ and write $q:E\oplus C^{n+1}\to P$ for its projection, $u=q\iota_E$ and $v=q\iota_{C^{n+1}}$. The relation is $uj=vd_C^n$. The cokernel universal property says precisely that $P$, with maps $u,v$, is the pushout of $j$ and $d_C^n$: a pair of maps out of $E,C^{n+1}$ descends exactly when it kills $(j,-d_C^n)$. Replace terms $C^n,C^{n+1}$ by $E,P$. The new differentials in degrees $n-1,n,n+1$ are $jd_C^{n-1}$, $u$, and the unique $g:P\to C^{n+2}$ satisfying $gq=(0,d_C^{n+1})$. This last map exists because $(0,d_C^{n+1})(j,-d_C^n)=0$. Their consecutive composites are zero: $ujd_C^{n-1}=vd_C^nd_C^{n-1}=0$, $gu=0$, and $d_C^{n+2}gq=(0,d_C^{n+2}d_C^{n+1})=0$; cancel the epi $q$ in the last identity. All other terms and arrows are retained. This defines a complex $C'$ and a chain map $f:C\to C'$ with components $j,v$ at $n,n+1$ and identities elsewhere, since $uj=vd_C^n$ and $gv=d_C^{n+1}$.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), elementary replacement diagram and its cokernel; the finite pushout description is homology.tex, Tag 05PJ (example-fibre-product-pushouts).

proof.text: The map $v$ of Step 3 is mono by [lem-weil-pbc-abelian-pushout-mono], applied to the pushout of the monomorphism $j$ along $d_C^n$. Thus $f$ is termwise mono. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-pushout-cokernel-iso] to the same square: the map $\theta:\operatorname{Coker}(j)\to\operatorname{Coker}(v)$ induced by $u$ is an isomorphism. Taking the componentwise cokernels of $f$ gives a quotient complex $Q$: its only possibly nonzero terms are $Q^n=\operatorname{Coker}(j)$ and $Q^{n+1}=\operatorname{Coker}(v)$, and its differential between them is exactly $\theta$ (this follows by composing with the cokernel projections). Therefore $H^r(Q)=0$ for every $r$: at $n$ the kernel of $\theta$ is zero, at $n+1$ its cokernel is zero, and elsewhere all terms are zero. The sequence $0\to C\xrightarrow f C'\to Q\to0$ is short exact in every degree. By [lem-weil-pbc-complex-ses-homology-long-exact], the adjacent zero terms $H^{r-1}(Q),H^r(Q)$ show that $H^r(f)$ is mono and epi, hence an isomorphism in the abelian category, for every $r$. Thus each elementary replacement is a quasi-isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), justification of the elementary replacement quasi-isomorphism; homology.tex Tags 08N4 (lemma-cartesian-cocartesian), 08N3 (lemma-cartesian-kernel), and 0117 (lemma-long-exact-sequence-cochain).

proof.text: The map $(j,-d_C^n)$ is mono because its first projection is mono. Apply the degree inequality to its short exact cokernel sequence to obtain $d(P)\leq\max\{d(C^n)-1,d(E\oplus C^{n+1})\}\leq\max\{d(C^n)-1,d(C^{n+1})\}$. Hence replacement makes degree $n$ zero, changes no other degree except $n+1$, and preserves the bound $d(C^r)\leq D$. Subtraction here is truncated, so the estimate also holds when $d(C^n)=1$ or $d(C^{n+1})=0$.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), numerical inequality after the elementary replacement diagram.

proof.text: For a complex $C$ reached from $J$, call an index bad if $d(C^n)>0$ and assign it weight $n+d(C^n)$. Initially bad indices lie below zero, and their weights are at most $D-1$. If there are bad indices, the nonempty set of their integer weights is bounded above and therefore has a largest element $\xi$. The indices $I$ attaining $\xi$ lie in the finite interval $[\xi-D,\xi-1]$. Make a replacement at the smallest index $n\in I$. Step 5 shows that every new bad weight is at most $\xi$: only $n+1$ can acquire a new one, and its new weight is at most $\max\{n+d(C^n),(n+1)+d(C^{n+1})\}$; if the old degree at $n+1$ is zero, use $n+1\leq\xi$ for the second term instead. The index $n$ leaves $I$, and only $n+1$ may enter it. Consequently, as long as the maximum stays $\xi$, the positive integer $\Phi=\sum_{r\in I}(\xi-r)$ drops by at least one: the removed contribution is $\xi-n$, and the only possible added contribution is $\xi-n-1$. After finitely many replacements there are no bad indices at weight $\xi$. Either none remain at all, or the maximum strictly decreases. This argument can be repeated at each new maximum; no maximum increases and the uniform bound $D$ is preserved.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), last proof paragraph, maximum weight and finite elimination of its attaining set; explicit decreasing integer for the source's termination argument.

proof.text: If $J$ has no bad indices, stop before the first round and take $L=J$ and $\beta=1_J$. Otherwise organize Step 6 into rounds, each consisting of the finitely many replacements that remove the current maximum weight. If a round leaves no bad terms, stop and retain that complex. Otherwise write $C_0=J,C_1,C_2,\ldots$ for the complexes at the beginnings of rounds and $\xi_s$ for their maximum weights. The finite composite $C_s\to C_{s+1}$ is a quasi-isomorphism by Step 4 and functoriality of cohomology, and $\xi_s\leq\xi_0-s$. A replacement within round $s$ has $n+d(C^n)=\xi_s$ with $d(C^n)\geq1$, so $n\leq\xi_s-1$. Its only changed terms are at $n,n+1\leq\xi_s$, its only changed differential sources are $n-1,n,n+1\leq\xi_s$, and its map is the identity outside those two terms. For any integer $m$, choose $s$ with $\xi_s<m$. No round from then on changes any term in degree $r\geq m$, any differential whose source has degree $r\geq m$, or any transition component in those degrees. Thus every right-hand tail is eventually literally unchanged; this uses finitely many rounds above any bound, not existence or exactness of an infinite colimit.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), last proof paragraph: ordering replacements so every brutal lower truncation changes only finitely often.

proof.text: In the infinite case define $L^r$ and $d_L^r$ to be the eventual values of the terms and arrows in Step 7. For any pair of consecutive arrows choose a round after which the three involved terms and these arrows are unchanged. Their composite is zero in that round, so it is zero in $L$. Hence $L$ is a cochain complex. The components of the composites $J\to C_s$ are eventually constant in every degree, since subsequent transition components there are identities; call the resulting family $\beta^r:J^r\to L^r$. Choose a common late round for degrees $r,r+1$ to see that $d_L^r\beta^r=\beta^{r+1}d_J^r$, so $\beta$ is a chain map. For fixed $r$, choose a round after stabilization in degree $r$ and with $\xi_s<r+1$. If the stabilized object $L^r=C_s^r$ had positive degree, its bad weight $r+d(C_s^r)\geq r+1$ would exceed $\xi_s$. Therefore $d(L^r)=0$. In the finite stopping case take the last complex and the finite composite as $L,\beta$; the same degree-zero conclusion holds by the stopping condition.

source.place: Tag 07K6 (lemma-replace-resolution), conclusion of the locally finite sequence of elementary replacements; explicit construction from the stabilized terms.

proof.text: Fix $r\in\mathbf Z$. In the infinite case choose a round $s$ after which the terms in degrees $r-1,r,r+1$ and their intervening differentials have stabilized. Under their eventual identifications, $H^r(L)=H^r(C_s)$, since both are the kernel of the same outgoing differential modulo the image of the same incoming one. The map $H^r(\beta)$ is exactly that of the finite composite $J\to C_s$, because the components in these three degrees have stabilized as well. It is an isomorphism by Step 4. In the finite stopping case $\beta$ is a finite composite of the quasi-isomorphisms of Step 4, or $1_J$ if there were no bad indices initially, so $H^r(\beta)$ is again an isomorphism. Thus $\beta$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Finally $K\xrightarrow\alpha J\xrightarrow\beta L$ is a quasi-isomorphism, since its map on each cohomology is the composite of two isomorphisms, and every term of $L$ has degree zero as required.
